title: The City of Bloodshed and the Empty Gap
summary: Ezekiel is told to put Jerusalem on trial as a city of bloodshed and to read out the charges: violence, idolatry, contempt for parents, exploitation of the foreigner, widow, and orphan, sexual sin, bribery, and usury. God will melt the city like dross in a furnace. The chapter ends with an indictment of every class of leaders, princes, priests, officials, prophets, and people, and God's lament that he looked for someone to stand in the gap and found no one.
story: Chapters 20 to 23 form a sustained case against Jerusalem in the last years before its fall. Chapter 20 told Israel's history; chapter 21 drew the sword; chapter 22 names the crimes that make the sword just. What stands out here is how ordinary many of the sins are. There is idolatry, but most of the list concerns how people treated one another: parents despised, widows and foreigners oppressed, neighbors defrauded, women abused. The chapter answers the question the exiles kept asking, why this is happening, by holding up the city's daily life. Its final image, the empty gap in the wall, prepares the reader for the siege that begins in chapter 24.
historical:
The chapter describes Jerusalem under Zedekiah, in the decade between the first deportation in 597 BC and the city's destruction in 587 or 586 BC. The prophet Jeremiah, preaching inside the city in those same years, brings many of the same charges: shedding innocent blood, oppressing the foreigner, orphan, and widow (Jeremiah 7:5-6; 22:3), and prophets who say peace when there is no peace (Jeremiah 6:14; 23:16-17).

The portrait of the city's leaders in verses 25 to 28 closely resembles Zephaniah 3:3-4, written a generation or two earlier in the reign of Josiah, where the officials are roaring lions, the judges evening wolves, the prophets reckless, and the priests profaners of the sanctuary. Ezekiel appears to take up that older oracle and show that nothing has changed. The expression the people of the land (verse 29) often refers in the books of Kings to the landowning citizens of Judah, who played a role in making and unmaking kings (2 Kings 11:14-20; 21:24; 23:30).
cultural:
The charges in verses 6 to 12 are drawn almost entirely from the Holiness Code of Leviticus 17 to 26, especially Leviticus 18 to 20, the part of the law most concerned with Israel living as a holy people. Honoring father and mother, protecting the foreigner, keeping the Sabbath, avoiding the forbidden sexual unions, refusing bribes and interest: these were the marks of a community that belonged to a holy God. For Ezekiel, a priest trained in these texts, the city's sins were a point-by-point reversal of its calling. Blood is the thread through the list, because shed blood was believed to pollute the land itself (Numbers 35:33).

The furnace image in verses 17 to 22 comes from ancient metalworking. Silver was refined by melting ore with lead and blowing air across it so that the base metals separated out as dross, leaving the silver behind. Ezekiel turns the process around: when Israel is put in the furnace, there is no silver to recover, only dross. The whitewash of verse 28 recalls 13:10-16, where false prophets smear whitewash over a flimsy wall to make it look sound.
literary: The chapter contains three oracles, each opening with the word of the LORD. The first (verses 1 to 16) is framed as a legal trial, with the prophet asked to judge the city and confront her with her abominations. Its list of charges is built around the repeated phrase in you or within you, placing each sin inside the city's walls. The second (verses 17 to 22) is a short extended metaphor of smelting. The third (verses 23 to 31) moves through the social order class by class, princes, priests, officials, prophets, and the people of the land, like a survey of every beam in a house and finding each one rotten. It ends with the image of the breach in the wall and the search for one person to stand in it, which turns the list of crimes into a moment of grief.

outline.t: The city of bloodshed put on trial
The charges: violence, contempt, oppression, sexual sin, greed
God strikes his hands: dispersion among the nations
Israel as dross in the furnace
Princes, priests, officials, prophets, and people all corrupt
No one found to stand in the gap

doctrines.note: The chapter shows sin as social as well as religious. Idolatry and injustice appear side by side, and the summary of all of them is in verse 12: they have forgotten God. Forgetting God shows itself in how the weak are treated.

The priests fail to distinguish between the holy and the common and between clean and unclean (verse 26). When the people charged with teaching holiness blur it, the whole community loses its bearings.

God's search for someone to stand in the gap (verse 30) assumes that intercession matters, that one person standing before God on behalf of the land could make a difference. Its absence is part of the tragedy.

words.note: Dam, blood, used eight times in this chapter. It usually refers here to shed blood, violence and murder, including judicial murder through bribery (verse 12). Jerusalem is named the city of bloodshed, literally city of bloods.

Sig, dross, the scum of base metal that separates from silver in the smelting fire. Isaiah uses the same image for Jerusalem (Isaiah 1:22, 25), though with a hope of refining. Ezekiel's version is bleaker: the whole house of Israel has become dross.

Ger, the foreign resident or sojourner, someone living in Israel without the protection of land or clan. The law repeatedly commands care for the ger, reminding Israel that they were foreigners in Egypt (Exodus 22:21). Their exploitation (verses 7 and 29) is a sign of the city's collapse.

Perets, a breach or gap in a wall. In siege warfare a breach was the point of greatest danger, and a soldier who stood in it risked everything. Psalm 106:23 uses the same image for Moses, who stood in the breach before God to turn away his wrath from Israel.

christ: The chapter ends with a man sought and not found. The prophets and psalms remember intercessors who stood between God's wrath and his people, above all Moses (Exodus 32:11-14; Psalm 106:23), and Ezekiel's lament is that in Jerusalem's last days no such person appeared. The New Testament presents Jesus as the one who stands in that place. He is the mediator between God and humanity (1 Timothy 2:5), who always lives to intercede for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25). Where Jerusalem's princes devoured the people and its priests blurred the holy, he is the king who gives his life for his people and the high priest who makes them holy. Ezekiel does not predict this; the link is the gap he names and the New Testament's claim about who fills it.

hard.q: God says he found no one to stand in the gap, but Jeremiah was in Jerusalem in those years. Was there really no one?
hard.a: Readers have noticed the problem. Jeremiah was a faithful prophet in the city, and others such as Baruch and Ebed-melech are presented as faithful too. Several answers are given. Many take verse 30 as prophetic totality, a way of saying that the society as a whole, its leaders and institutions, had no one able to turn it; Jeremiah 5:1 has a similar search for one person in Jerusalem who does justice. Others note that the man sought is someone with the standing to repair the wall, a leader who could turn the nation, which Jeremiah, persecuted and imprisoned, was not allowed to be. Still others point to Jeremiah's own record: God repeatedly told him not to pray for the people (Jeremiah 7:16; 11:14; 14:11), a sign that the time for intercession to avert the disaster had passed. The chapter does not deny that faithful individuals existed; it says that none could stand in the breach and turn the city from its course.

questions: Most of the sins in verses 6 to 12 concern how people treated parents, foreigners, widows, and neighbors. What would a similar list say about your community?
Every class of leader failed at once in verses 25 to 29. How does corruption at one level of a society make it easier at others?
What would it mean for you to stand in the gap for your family, church, or city before God?
